\section{Introduction}
OrthoHPI 2.0 renews and extends the original OrthoHPI
resource~\cite{cuestaastroz2019analysis}, integrating current releases of the
underlying databases and predictors and broadening the set of parasites
covered. Host proteins are restricted to surface-exposed localisations
predicted by DeepLoc~\cite{dum2024deeploc}.

\todo{introduction}

\section{Methods}

% The stages below mirror docs/pipeline.md, which is the running description
% of what `python -m pipeline.main` actually does. Keep the two in step.

Figure~\ref{fig:workflow} gives an overview of the prediction workflow: the
host and parasite proteomes are filtered by tissue expression and predicted
subcellular localisation, and interactions are then transferred between the
remaining proteins through shared orthologous groups.

% paper/figures/workflow.png is exported from workflow.svg: `make figures`.
\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/workflow}
  \caption{Overview of the OrthoHPI 2.0 prediction workflow. For each
  host--parasite pair, the host proteome is restricted to proteins expressed in
  the tissues the parasite infects (TISSUES) and to localisations the parasite
  can reach (DeepLoc), and the parasite proteome to extracellular and, for
  unicellular parasites, cell-membrane proteins. STRING interactions between
  EggNOG orthologous groups are transferred to the remaining host and parasite
  proteins, each predicted pair scored by the mean of the experimental and
  database evidence scores.}
  \label{fig:workflow}
\end{figure}

\section{Results}

\subsection{The predicted networks}
\todo{Size of the networks; what drives the spread between parasites.}
Figure~\ref{fig:networks} shows the size of each predicted network and where in
the host cell its interactions land.

% paper/figures/networks.pdf is generated: `make figures` (see Makefile).
\begin{figure}[p]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.83\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/networks}
  \caption{Predicted interactions of every host--parasite pair, one block per
  host, the blocks sharing an axis so that a bar is comparable across hosts.
  Each bar is split by where DeepLoc places the host protein: on the surface
  (extracellular or cell membrane), in the interior (cytoplasm or nucleus), or
  called for both. The interior fraction is what the parasite's niche opens to
  it, so it is substantial only for the intracellular parasites. The strips
  beside the names give the niche (outer) and the taxonomic group (inner).}
  \label{fig:networks}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:funnel} quantifies the filters of Figure~\ref{fig:workflow},
stage by stage and separately for each host--parasite pair, as the share of
proteins each stage keeps. The DeepLoc filter keeps 77--84\% of the host
proteins expressed in the infected tissues for an intracellular parasite,
against 18--26\% for an extracellular one.

% paper/figures/funnel_shares.png is generated: `make figures` (see Makefile).
\begin{figure}[p]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.83\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/funnel_shares}
  \caption{Share of proteins each stage of the pipeline keeps, for every
  host--parasite pair, one row per pair in blocks by host. Each coloured cell is
  the percentage of proteins kept from the stage before. Host side: expressed in
  a tissue the parasite infects (TISSUES) of the STRING proteome, in a reachable
  localisation (DeepLoc) of those, in a KOG group of those, and in a predicted
  interaction (PPI) of those. Parasite side: secreted or on the surface
  (DeepLoc) of the STRING proteome, in a KOG group of those, and in a predicted
  interaction (PPI) of those. Both filters keep what
  Figure~\ref{fig:workflow} specifies; only the KOG groups of EggNOG carry
  interactions in STRING, so only their members can be linked. The grey counts
  give the size of the parasite's STRING proteome and the number of predicted
  interactions of the pair; the size of the host's proteome follows its name.
  Rows are ordered by the parasite's niche in the host, then taxonomic group,
  then name; the strips beside the names give the niche (outer) and the
  taxonomic group (inner). The counts behind every cell are in Supplementary
  Table~S1.}
  \label{fig:funnel}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Structural models of the transferred interactions}
\todo{Interpretation; cite AlphaFold 3 and ipSAE.}
Figure~\ref{fig:alphafold_direct} compares AlphaFold 3 models of 48 predicted
links from 25 parasites against models of the human interactions they were
transferred from. Of the 20 human references with an ipSAE interface, the
predicted link reproduces it in 6; ipTM finds an interface in one pair only.

% paper/figures/alphafold_direct.png is generated: `make figures`.
\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/alphafold_direct}
  \caption{AlphaFold 3 interface confidence of predicted parasite--human links
  against that of the human interaction each was transferred from. The 48 links
  are predicted against human, eight from each confidence-score bin between 0.35
  and 1, at most one per pair of orthologous groups. Each is paired with a human
  reference: a pair of human members of the same two orthologous groups shown to
  bind directly in BioGRID or IntAct, the predicted human partner itself where
  possible (circles), otherwise the pair with the most publications (diamonds).
  \textbf{(A)} ipTM and \textbf{(B)} ipSAE of the best-ranked model of each
  complex, coloured by the confidence score of the link. The dashed lines mark
  an interface as found (ipTM $\ge 0.6$, ipSAE $\ge 0.1$), and the counts give
  the links in each quadrant: an interface in both models, only in the
  reference, only in the predicted link, or in neither.}
  \label{fig:alphafold_direct}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Parasites of the same host reach overlapping host proteins}
\todo{Interpretation: similarity within genera and within niches.}
Figure~\ref{fig:similarity} compares the interactomes of the parasites of human
pair by pair, Figure~\ref{fig:shared_families} the host families that the
most of them converge on, and Figure~\ref{fig:parasite_go} the host processes
they reach. The processes split by niche rather than by taxonomy: the
intracellular parasites, \textit{Trichinella} among them, reach host proteins of
RNA splicing, ribonucleoprotein biogenesis and autophagy, and the extracellular
ones host proteins of cell adhesion, integrin signalling and lipid metabolism.
\todo{Check the niche split against the literature; note that each parasite is
tested against its own niche's pool.}

% paper/figures/parasite_similarity.pdf is generated: `make figures`.
\begin{figure}[p]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.83\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/parasite_similarity}
  \caption{Jaccard similarity of the sets of human proteins reached by each
  pair of parasites predicted against human. Parasites are ordered by niche in
  the host, then taxonomic group, then name, so that the two niches read as
  blocks; the strips along both axes give the niche (outer) and the taxonomic
  group (inner), and the diagonal is left grey. Similarity is highest within a
  genus and falls away sharply between the niches, which draw on different host
  localisations.}
  \label{fig:similarity}
\end{figure}

% paper/figures/shared_families.pdf is generated: `make figures`.
\begin{figure}[p]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.83\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/shared_families}
  \caption{Host protein families of human reached by at least 24
  parasites, as a dot matrix over the parasites predicted against human. A
  family is the orthologous group of the host protein, labelled by the gene
  symbols of its members, and is reached by a parasite when any parasite
  protein is predicted to interact with any member. The area of a dot is the
  number of parasite proteins reaching that family, drawn at 20 for more. The two columns on the
  right count the parasites reaching the family and the distinct parasite
  orthologous groups they do so through --- one group means a single conserved
  parasite protein transferred many times, rather than independent
  convergence. The strips above the matrix
  give the niche (outer) and the taxonomic group (inner).}
  \label{fig:shared_families}
\end{figure}

% paper/figures/parasite_go.pdf is generated: `make figures`.
\begin{figure}[p]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.83\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/parasite_go}
  \caption{Gene Ontology biological processes over-represented among the human
  proteins each parasite is predicted to reach. Each parasite is tested on its own
  with a one-sided Fisher's exact test against the human proteins of its niche that
  passed the pipeline's filters, and corrected with Benjamini--Hochberg; a dot marks
  a process at FDR $\le 0.05$, its area the number of the parasite's host
  interactors annotated to the process and its shade the odds ratio. The odds ratio
  is shaded rather than the FDR, which follows how many interactors a parasite has.
  For each parasite, its most significant processes are taken in turn until two are
  represented; a process is merged into an already shown row when the two share half
  or more of their combined human proteins (Jaccard index $\ge 0.5$). Rows are
  ordered by hierarchical clustering of which parasites they are enriched for, so
  processes enriched for similar parasites sit together. Parasites are ordered by
  niche, then taxonomic group, then name, with the niche (outer) and taxonomic group
  (inner) in the strips above the matrix. All predictions at confidence score $\ge 0.35$; every enriched process
  of every parasite is in Supplementary Table~\todo{table}.}
  \label{fig:parasite_go}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Comparing the hosts of one parasite}
\todo{Interpretation: how much of a parasite's interactome is host specific.}
Figure~\ref{fig:multi_host} compares, for each parasite predicted against more
than one host, which interactions are shared and why the others are missing.

% paper/figures/multi_host.pdf is generated: `make figures`.
\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/multi_host}
  \caption{Hosts compared for every parasite predicted against more than one.
  An interaction is compared between hosts as the pair of orthologous groups it
  was transferred from, so a link counts as shared when both hosts carry a
  protein of the host group interacting with the parasite's. \textbf{(A)} The
  links of each parasite, split by the hosts carrying them. \textbf{(B)} For
  each host, the links it lacks that another host of the same parasite carries,
  attributed to the first filter the host family fails there: the family is
  absent from the host proteome, the TISSUES filter keeps no member in a tissue
  the parasite infects, or the DeepLoc filter keeps no remaining member in a
  location the parasite reaches. Every missing link falls into one of these
  three; none is a family that passes every filter and carries no transferred
  link, since a link is transferred at the level of the orthologous group. The
  last two causes reflect the coverage of TISSUES and the accuracy of DeepLoc
  for that host as much as the biology of the host family.}
  \label{fig:multi_host}
\end{figure}

\todo{Interpretation of the \textit{Leishmania braziliensis} case study.}
Figure~\ref{fig:lb_case_study} compares the \textit{Leishmania braziliensis}
networks of human and mouse.

% paper/figures/lb_case_study.png is generated: `make figures`.
\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/lb_case_study}
  \caption{\textit{Leishmania braziliensis} in human and mouse, its links
  compared between the hosts as in Figure~\ref{fig:multi_host}.
  \textbf{(A)} The body figure of each host, as in the OrthoHPI app, its
  infected organs shaded by the number of predicted interactions whose host
  protein TISSUES annotates to them, given under each figure; of the tissues
  the parasite infects, the figures draw skin and blood, but not nose, mouth
  or macrophages. \textbf{(B)} The links of each host, shared with the other
  or found only in it, the latter split by the filter that removes the host
  family in the other host. \textbf{(C, D)} The host families linked to two
  parasite families, the autophagy-related protein ATG8 (C) and the surface
  protease leishmanolysin, GP63 (D), in each host (rows). A column is a host family,
  named by the genes of its members carrying a link; a cell is coloured by the
  best confidence score of the link in that host, and a host lacking the link
  is marked by the filter removing its family there (T, TISSUES; L, DeepLoc).
  (C) shows the 22 best-scoring of the 28 host families linked to ATG8.}
  \label{fig:lb_case_study}
\end{figure}

\subsection{From parasite protein to host cell type}
\todo{Interpretation of the \textit{Plasmodium falciparum} case study.}
Figure~\ref{fig:pf_case_study} narrows the \textit{Plasmodium falciparum}
network to the host proteins of the liver stage.

% paper/figures/pf_case_study.png is generated: `make figures`.
\begin{figure}[p]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.83\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/pf_case_study}
  \caption{\textit{Plasmodium falciparum} in \textit{Homo sapiens}, narrowed
  in stages: the predicted interactions with a confidence score of at least
  0.7 (A); those whose host protein is found in the liver (B); and from these
  two branches, those whose host protein is enhanced in hepatocytes (C),
  following the Human Protein Atlas definition of cell type enhanced (detected
  at more than 1 normalized transcript per million, nTPM, and at least four
  times its mean nTPM over the other cell types) applied within the liver cell
  types of its single-cell RNA-seq data \todo{cite Digre and Lindskog 2023},
  and those whose host protein is found in none of the other tissues the
  parasite infects, namely skin, blood, brain and spleen (D).
  \textbf{(A--D)} The network of each stage, drawn as in the OrthoHPI app:
  parasite proteins as diamonds, host proteins as circles, and link width by
  confidence score. In (A) and (B), proteins and links that reach no later
  stage are greyed. In (C) and (D), a parasite protein is named by its
  STRING description, or by its gene name where it has none, and a host protein
  by its gene name. \textbf{(E)} Gene Ontology biological processes enriched
  among the host proteins of each stage (Fisher's exact test against the host
  proteins the pipeline could have predicted, Benjamini--Hochberg FDR $<$
  0.05); each stage contributes its three best terms, leaving out a term
  covering the same host proteins as a better one.}
  \label{fig:pf_case_study}
\end{figure}

\section*{Supplementary material}
\textbf{Supplementary Table S1} (\texttt{funnel\_supplementary.csv}). One row
per host--parasite pair, in the order Figure~\ref{fig:funnel} draws them: the
host and parasite proteins surviving each stage of the pipeline, and the number
of predicted interactions of the pair. Supplied as a comma-separated file
rather than typeset, since the 56 rows are meant to be sorted and filtered.

\textbf{Supplementary Figure S1}. Confidence scores of the predicted
interactions of each host--parasite pair (Figure~\ref{fig:confidence}).

% paper/figures/confidence.pdf is generated: `make figures` (see Makefile).
\begin{figure}[p]
  \captionsetup{name=Supplementary Figure}
  \renewcommand{\thefigure}{S1}
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.83\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/confidence}
  \caption{Confidence scores of the predicted interactions of every
  host--parasite pair, laid out as Figure~\ref{fig:networks}: one block per
  host, one box per parasite. The score of a prediction is the average of the
  experimental and database evidence of the KOG--KOG link it was transferred
  from; a link is kept only if one of the two is at least 0.7, so no score is
  below 0.35. Boxes span the interquartile range with the median marked,
  whiskers extend to 1.5 times the interquartile range, and outliers are not
  drawn. \textit{T.~hominis} has a single prediction. The strips beside the
  names give the niche (outer) and the taxonomic group (inner).}
  \label{fig:confidence}
\end{figure}
